query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a rapid quenching intervention (i.e., a high-rate cooling process) to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will improve their glass‐forming ability and thermal stability relative to samples produced under slow cooling conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: The alloy in a near-molten or fully molten state, specifically a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
generation.intervention: Implement a rapid cooling process (e.g., melt-spinning or an accelerated cooling method via an electric arc pulse) immediately after melting.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be applied under controlled inert atmospheres at a cooling rate in the range of 10^5–10^6 K/s, while the baseline involves traditional slow cooling (~50 K/s). This is expected to work in phosphorus-rich alloys with high mixing entropy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a homogeneous amorphous structure with reduced short-range order in comparison to a multi-phase crystalline structure.
generation.mechanism: Rapid quenching minimizes the time available for atomic rearrangements, thereby suppressing the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases. This kinetic suppression enhances the glass-forming ability while also elevating the thermal stability of the amorphous phase by delaying crystallization upon heating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to rapid cooling will exhibit a higher amorphous content (as evidenced by XRD and microscopy), and differential scanning calorimetry will show an elevated onset of crystallization, indicating improved thermal stability compared to samples cooled slowly.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed via slow cooling, which tend to form complex crystalline microstructures with lower glass-forming ability and less thermally stable amorphous regions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected primarily in alloys with significant phosphorus content and high configurational entropy. It may be less effective or require modification in alloys with very different compositions or when additional micro-alloying elements dominate the transformation kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The critical cooling rate required to guarantee a fully amorphous structure and the precise quantitative improvements in thermal stability remain uncertain and are likely influenced by the detailed alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy from an identical melt state. For one set, apply traditional slow cooling (approximately 50 K/s). For the second set, subject the alloy to rapid cooling (using a technique such as melt-spinning to achieve rates near 10^5–10^6 K/s). Ensure that all other processing parameters are kept constant.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to determine the presence or absence of crystalline phases.
Scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructural analysis.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the onset temperature of crystallization (thermal stability).
Quantification of amorphous content via techniques such as synchrotron radiation or atom probe tomography if applicable.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the rapidly cooled samples do not show a statistically significant increase in amorphous content and/or do not demonstrate a higher crystallization onset temperature relative to the slow-cooled baseline. A lack of at least a modest (e.g., >10%) improvement in these measurements would challenge the proposed mechanism.

## Abstract
This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. ## Abstract
AbstractWhile the concept of high entropy has gained prominence in materials design, disentangling specific impacts of entropy on material properties from the enthalpy of mixing remains elusive. It is demonstrated that the role of entropy can be distinguished from the dynamics of glass‐forming liquids through micro‐alloying. Based on experiment analysis of 79 compositions, liquid fragility is found to consistently decreases under two conditions: i) when the alloying content x is minimal, irrespective of the elements used; or ii) when increasing the diversity of alloying elements at a constant x, namely the high‐entropy micro‐alloying. These observations are consistent with thermodynamic principles that favor an entropy‐dominated regime over enthalpy. These findings elucidate the subtle impact of mixing entropy on material properties and provide evidence of the entropy nature of glass transition. This research innovates by distinguishing entropy’s impact from enthalpy in materials through micro‐alloying.
